turns.zh: 所以如果演讲到此结束，我就不会谈论为什么我们可能在一年内面临严重问题。我会谈论为什么我们可能在四年或八年内面临严重问题。这次演讲之所以如此紧迫，是因为我们开始看到 AI 开发过程本身的自动化。我的意思是，如果我们看看我刚才提到的过去四年或八年 AI 的进步，其中很大一部分是由扩展到更大系统驱动的，但很大一部分也是由人类做研究、提出新的聪明想法驱动的。我认为如果你回顾过去 8 年，你可能会估计大约一半的进步来自新想法。如果你看更近期的，我想大多数研究人员会同意这个比例更大。所以，我们确实在训练越来越大的 AI 系统，但我们也越来越擅长训练它们。因此，即使你看固定成本水平的系统，它们的性能也一直在极速提升。达到任何给定性能水平的成本一直在下降。

turns.en: One of the major goals of AI companies, and particularly Anthropic and OpenAI, is to automate that research. So say instead of humans coming up with those ideas, we would like machines to come up with those ideas. This is an essay by Anthropic talking about their progress towards recursive self-improvement. This is a job posting by OpenAI recruiting researchers to come automate the role of a researcher at OpenAI. This is one of the big things we—the companies—are trying to do that we as a civilization are effectively directing so many resources towards.
turns.zh: AI 公司的主要目标之一，尤其是 Anthropic 和 OpenAI，就是自动化这项研究。也就是说，与其由人类提出那些想法，我们希望机器来提出那些想法。这是 Anthropic 的一篇文章，谈论他们在递归自我改进方面的进展。这是 OpenAI 的一则招聘启事，招募研究人员来自动化 OpenAI 研究员的角色。这是这些公司正在努力做的一件大事，而我们作为一个文明实际上正将如此多的资源导向此事。

turns.en: So against that backdrop—that this is sort of the plan, this is what people are trying to achieve—we are in fact seeing AI agents getting very good at benchmarks of their ability to do automated R&D. This is a graph METR maintained over several years, although it's roughly retired now, showing the length of task that AI systems are able to autonomously pursue. So this graph shows systems moving up from doing tasks that would have taken humans a minute or two, to doing tasks that would have taken humans an hour or two, to now doing tasks that would take humans a day or two.
turns.zh: 所以在这种背景下——这就是计划，这就是人们试图实现的目标——我们实际上看到 AI 智能体在自动化研发能力的基准上表现得非常好。这是 METR 维护了数年的图表，尽管现在大致已退役，它显示了 AI 系统能够自主追求的任务长度。所以这张图显示系统从完成人类需要一两分钟的任务，到完成人类需要一两小时的任务，到现在完成人类需要一两天才能完成的任务。

turns.en: The reason the graph has been retired is it gets very hard to build this graph for tasks that take humans a week or two or a month or two. So people are increasingly relying on other evaluation methodologies because it's so hard to construct benchmarks in these areas. You see similar results across essentially every benchmark in this area. Benchmarks that were constructed to be as hard as we could possibly make them are rapidly getting saturated. At this point, there are essentially no benchmarks we can use to measure the rate of progress.
turns.zh: 这张图之所以被弃用，是因为对于需要人类花费一两周或一两个月完成的任务，构建这样的图变得非常困难。因此人们越来越依赖其他评估方法，因为在这些领域构建基准实在太难了。在这个领域的几乎每一个基准上，你都能看到类似的结果。那些我们尽可能构建得最难的基准正在迅速饱和。到了这个阶段，我们基本上已经没有基准可以用来衡量进展速度了。

turns.en: We can then look at what is actually happening in the labs. So how much are people adopting AI? This is a graph OpenAI published on how much internal coding agent activity there was for each researcher. And what you see is over the course of just this calendar year, you have increased from a very very low level to a significant fraction of the salary of the humans involved. This does not imply that AI systems are working well. It is completely plausible that from this graph that OpenAI is making a terrible mistake and deploying a bunch of systems that don't really work. But it is certainly the case that they are deploying them.
turns.zh: 然后我们可以看看实验室里实际发生了什么。人们采用 AI 的程度有多高？这是 OpenAI 发布的一张图，展示了每位研究员的内部编码智能体活动量。你可以看到，仅仅在这个日历年内，就从非常非常低的水平增长到了相当于相关人员薪资的相当大一部分。这并不意味着 AI 系统运行良好。完全有可能从这张图看出 OpenAI 犯了一个可怕的错误，部署了一堆并不真正有效的系统。但可以肯定的是，他们正在部署这些系统。

turns.en: This is a graph Anthropic published showing if you look back on tasks AI systems were asked to do within the company, how often did the AI system succeed? And again looking over something like a year you moved from a world where most of the time systems failed at tasks human gave them to most of the time it kind of at least looks like the system succeeded. So this complements what we see from evidence in R&D benchmarks. We're both seeing performance looks good on benchmarks in the lab. We are also seeing very rapid adoption. Right? These curves show doubling over every month or two of adoption, not every year or two.
turns.zh: 这是 Anthropic 发布的一张图，展示了回顾公司内部要求 AI 系统完成的任务时，AI 系统成功的频率如何。同样，在大约一年的时间里，你从一个系统大多数时候在人类交给它们的任务上失败的世界，变成了大多数时候至少看起来系统成功了的世界。所以这补充了我们在研发基准中看到的证据。我们既看到实验室基准上的性能看起来不错，也看到非常快速的采用。对吧？这些曲线显示采用量每一两个月就翻一番，而不是每一两年。

turns.en: Now I want to step back a little bit from machine learning and talk about what we've experienced in mathematics over the last few months. I expect many people in the audience have followed this at least from a distance if not up close. If we look back two years to autumn of 2024, Terrence Tao described 01 as being like a mediocre grad student who could go look some stuff up for you, who could maybe do some simple work, but who was not able to drive results autonomously very effectively. In autumn of 2025, mathematicians still mostly use AI systems as assistants, though we're not really changing the way mathematics was practiced very deeply. There were a few autonomous results, but these were more like curiosities than actually meaningful contributions to the field.
turns.zh: 现在我想从机器学习稍微退一步，谈谈过去几个月我们在数学领域的经历。我预计在座的许多人至少从远处关注过这件事，如果不是近距离的话。如果我们回顾两年前，也就是 2024 年秋天，陶哲轩把 01 描述为一个平庸的研究生，能帮你查些资料，也许能做点简单的工作，但无法非常有效地自主推动结果。到了 2025 年秋天，数学家仍然主要把 AI 系统当作助手，并没有真正深刻地改变数学的实践方式。有一些自主的结果，但这些更像是奇闻趣事，而不是对该领域真正有意义的贡献。

turns.en: Around 6 months ago, in spring of 2026, we saw perhaps the first real substantial result that was delivered by automated mathematicians. And then this fall, we have seen hundreds of huge math results. So if you look say in my area of mathematics I would say that the progress we saw in October of 2026 was larger than the progress we saw in the preceding decade. So we had AI systems which not only surpassed humans but resulted in radically faster progress on the hardest problems in the field than humans had been able to make. I think for many people this was an extremely alarming warning shot.
turns.zh: 大约 6 个月前，也就是 2026 年春天，我们看到了或许是由自动化数学家交付的第一个真正实质性的结果。然后到了今年秋天，我们看到了数百个重大的数学成果。所以如果你看比如我的数学领域，我会说我们在 2026 年 10 月看到的进展比之前十年看到的进展还要大。所以我们有了不仅超越人类，而且在该领域最难的问题上带来了比人类所能取得的进展快得多的 AI 系统。我认为对许多人来说，这是一个极其令人警觉的警告信号。

turns.en: I think the question that is natural is what if the same thing happened in machine learning. Right? So machine learning is a domain which like math is very well suited to automation, right? It is an activity that occurs entirely within the data center almost by definition. It is an activity where the goal is to make a number go up where you can tell if you succeeded or if you failed. And so it is in principle an activity that might see similar gains to automation. There are big differences, right? Machine learning is messier than mathematics and more importantly machine learning is bottlenecked by the available compute in a way that mathematics is not. So this makes it more challenging. On the other hand, the level of investment in automating machine learning is significantly larger than the level of investment in automating mathematics. And if you look at where this nets out, it looks like we are lagging somewhere behind, but more like a year behind than a couple years behind.
turns.zh: 我认为自然的问题是，如果同样的事情发生在机器学习领域会怎样。对吧？机器学习是一个像数学一样非常适合自动化的领域。它几乎按定义就是完全在数据中心内进行的活动。它是一个目标就是让某个数字上升的活动，你能分辨自己是成功还是失败。所以原则上它可能看到与自动化类似的收益。但也有很大的不同，对吧？机器学习比数学更混乱，更重要的是机器学习在某种程度上受限于可用算力，而数学则不是。所以这使它更具挑战性。另一方面，在自动化机器学习上的投资水平显著大于在自动化数学上的投资水平。如果你看最终结果，看起来我们落后一些，但更像是一年而不是几年。

turns.en: And if you were to see something similar, if you were to see AI coming up with 10 years worth of ideas, it seems like the impact would be larger than the impact we've seen from like GPT3 to GPT6, right? This would be a very large change in the capabilities of AI systems. This would mean things that we were extrapolating might only appear in four years or eight years could instead appear over a very short period of time.
turns.zh: 如果你看到类似的事情，如果你看到 AI 提出了相当于 10 年量的想法，那么影响似乎会比我们从 GPT3 到 GPT6 看到的影响更大，对吧？这将是 AI 系统能力的非常大的变化。这意味着我们之前外推可能在四年或八年后才出现的东西，反而可能在非常短的时间内出现。

turns.en: Things can get even more extreme than this. Right? So if you imagine that AI systems are being deployed primarily or in significant part to accelerate the further progress in AI and you see that over some period of 12 months AI systems take over the AI development process and progress in proving those AI systems doubles the rate of progress. Right? If you went into that world where the future developments arrive twice as quickly as previous developments, you would then ask what happens next? What should we expect looking forward from that point after those 12 months? And if really the thing that drove change over those 12 months was new ideas in machine learning was progress in machine learning, then you might expect that the same change would occur next time over six months instead. Right? Things are not really going to be this simple. But to first order, if the thing driving AI progress is the development of new ideas and each unit of AI improvement makes it faster to develop new ideas, each unit of progress becomes faster. And you might see that process occur again and that process occur again.
turns.zh: 事情甚至可以比这更极端。对吧？所以如果你想象 AI 系统主要或很大一部分被部署来加速 AI 的进一步进展，并且你看到在 12 个月的时间里，AI 系统接管了 AI 开发过程，并且在改进这些 AI 系统方面的进展使进展速度翻倍。对吧？如果你进入那个世界，未来的发展以两倍于先前发展的速度到来，你然后会问接下来会发生什么？从那 12 个月之后的那个点向前看，我们应该期待什么？如果真正推动那 12 个月变化的是机器学习中的新想法，是机器学习的进步，那么你可能预期同样的变化下次会在六个月内发生。对吧？事情不会真的这么简单。但一阶近似下，如果推动 AI 进步的是新想法的发展，而每一单位的 AI 改进都使发展新想法更快，那么每一单位的进步都变得更快。你可能会看到这个过程再次发生，然后再次发生。

turns.en: This is on top of this basic concern, right? That if you do very well, if you see the same thing in machine learning as you saw in mathematics, you might make a fairly large unit of progress very quickly as you cross the level of humans who are doing this research themselves.
turns.zh: 这是在这个基本担忧之上的，对吧？如果你做得非常好，如果你在机器学习中看到与数学中相同的事情，你可能会在跨越从事这项研究的人类水平时，非常迅速地取得相当大的进展。

turns.en: So, a lot of attention has been paid to this graph published by Anthropic and METR last week. So what you're seeing on screen is an aggregate of capability benchmarks that Anthropic uses to measure progress internally. This is a time series broken about one year ago. You see that bend in the curve. This is not a very scientific or clever curve fit. This is just the most simple thing you could do. But for a variety of ways of extrapolating this trend, you do see that progress over the last year is significantly faster than progress during the preceding period. That's coupled with asking machine learning researchers across many labs how fast you feel like you're going. And researchers report feeling like they are moving significantly faster because of AI automation. So we are seeing systems performing well on benchmarks being broadly adopted.
turns.zh: 所以，很多人关注了 Anthropic 和 METR 上周发布的这张图。你在屏幕上看到的是 Anthropic 内部用来衡量进展的能力基准的汇总。这是一个在大约一年前出现断点的时间序列。你看到曲线中的那个弯折。这不是非常科学或巧妙的曲线拟合。这只是你能做的最简单的事情。但用多种方式外推这个趋势，你确实看到过去一年的进展显著快于之前那段时期的进展。这与询问许多实验室的机器学习研究人员你感觉进展有多快相结合。研究人员报告说，由于 AI 自动化，他们感觉进展显著加快。所以我们看到在基准上表现良好的系统正在被广泛采用。

turns.en: People in surveys saying that they feel like their work has been greatly accelerated and some quantitative metrics showing that progress is in fact accelerating. I think from this graph alone it's very hard to know what you should expect going forward. Right? There are huge number of limitations both of the y-axis and of understanding what is driving progress in this graph.
turns.zh: 调查中的人们表示他们觉得自己的工作被大大加速了，还有一些量化指标显示进展确实在加速。我认为仅从这张图很难知道未来应该预期什么。对吧？y 轴和对于这张图中推动进展的因素的理解都存在大量限制。

turns.en: So I think this is a really unfortunate aspect of the current situation is most of the evidence necessary to really know what you should expect over the next 3 months or 6 months is held as closely held proprietary information by AI developers. So we are right now in a regime where it is extremely hard for someone to make a reasonable forecast based on public information.
turns.zh: 所以我认为当前情况的一个非常不幸的方面是，真正了解未来 3 个月或 6 个月应该预期什么所需的大部分证据，都被 AI 开发者作为严格保密的专有信息持有。所以我们现在处于一个极其难以基于公开信息做出合理预测的状态。

turns.en: So in this case, part of why this update was impactful for many people is three researchers from Meter spent a few weeks at Anthropic reviewing private evidence. And though they were not allowed to publish the results, they offered the same bottom line that if you look at more fine-grained output measures and more careful input measures, you see a similar pattern of acceleration.
turns.zh: 所以在这种情况下，这次更新对许多人产生冲击的部分原因是，来自 Meter 的三位研究员在 Anthropic 待了几周审查私有证据。尽管他们不被允许发表结果，但他们给出了相同的底线结论：如果你看更细粒度的输出指标和更仔细的输入指标，你会看到类似的加速模式。

turns.en: I think it is really unfortunate that we're in a place where people are trying to rely on three researchers from an independent organization to review that data if it actually ends up being a really critical question about the future of the field.
turns.zh: 我认为我们落到这样一个境地真的很不幸：如果这最终成为关乎该领域未来的关键问题，人们却要依赖一个独立组织的三位研究员来审查那些数据。

turns.en: However, I would say we are seeing what you might expect to see at the beginning of a process of acceleration or shortly before you saw 10 years of progress compressed into a short period of time.
turns.zh: 然而，我想说我们看到的正是你在加速过程开始时可能预期看到的现象，或者是在你看到 10 年的进展被压缩到短时间之前不久。

turns.en: You could then ask if there is this acceleration, how far does that acceleration actually go? Right? We know at some point AI progress will slow down and maybe it won't slow down by default in the next year, but it's going to slow down at some point.
turns.zh: 然后你可以问，如果存在这种加速，这种加速实际上能走多远？对吧？我们知道在某个时候 AI 进展会放缓，也许明年不会自动放缓，但总会在某个时候放缓。

turns.en: I think a way you could think about that question is to look back over history. Uh, you know, you might expect something to continue going about as long as it has gone so far. That's a very stupid heuristic, but I do think it's a good starting point if you want to try and think about the future.
turns.zh: 我认为思考这个问题的一种方式是回顾历史。呃，你知道，你可能会预期某事物持续的时间大约与它迄今为止持续的时间一样长。这是一个非常愚蠢的启发式，但我确实认为如果你想尝试思考未来，这是一个好的起点。

turns.en: In deep learning, we have seen rapid progress for roughly the last 10 years. Maybe depending on how you'd argue, you could say much longer than that. Um, and we have not seen signs of slowdown. If anything, I would say on many metrics, it looks like progress has somewhat accelerated over those 10 years.
turns.zh: 在深度学习中，我们在大约过去 10 年里看到了快速进展。也许取决于你怎么论证，你可以说比那长得多。呃，而且我们没有看到放缓的迹象。如果说有什么不同的话，我想说在许多指标上，进展在这 10 年里似乎有所加速。

turns.en: At the same time, AI systems are not limited to the problem of doing deep learning better. Right? Over the long broader history of AI, we have worked with a number of different techniques. Humans have tried to come up with the best ideas we can. But as we saw in math, we may soon be in the regime where AI systems are able to come up with ideas that would have taken the community of human experts many decades.
turns.zh: 与此同时，AI 系统并不局限于更好地做深度学习这个问题。对吧？在 AI 更漫长的历史中，我们使用过许多不同的技术。人类已经尽力想出最好的想法。但正如我们在数学中看到的，我们可能很快进入这样一个状态：AI 系统能够提出人类专家群体需要几十年才能想到的想法。

turns.en: And so AI may find new approaches to progress, further extending how much progress we see before hitting enough diminishing returns to slow the dynamic.
turns.zh: 因此，AI 可能会找到新的进展途径，进一步延长我们看到进展的时间，直到遇到足够的收益递减来减缓这一动态。

turns.en: I would say between all of this, it looks not a sure thing at all, but reasonably likely that we will see another 10 years of progress before we have slowdowns. And again, the purpose of that is to say if we look back at these long-term trends that puts us at a very alarming level of capability.
turns.zh: 我想说，综合所有这些，这看起来根本不是确定的事，但相当有可能我们会再看到 10 年的进展才会出现放缓。再说一次，这样说的目的是，如果我们回顾这些长期趋势，那将使我们处于一个非常令人警觉的能力水平。

turns.en: So I'm going to talk through a couple objections, reasons this may not occur, which are important considerations. So one is that unlike math, machine learning has compute bottlenecks. In order to do research, you need to run experiments. If you try and do research faster and faster, those compute bottlenecks become more and more intense.
turns.zh: 所以我要讨论几个反对意见，即这不会发生的理由，这些是重要的考虑因素。其一，与数学不同，机器学习存在算力瓶颈。为了做研究，你需要运行实验。如果你试图越来越快地做研究，那些算力瓶颈会变得越来越严重。

turns.en: So you can try and look at data from machine learning R&D and estimate are we in the regime where you should expect the sort of progress to be self-sustaining where you should see this acceleration that becomes super exponential or are we in a regime where the bottleneck should eventually become binding and the rate of progress should be bottlenecked by the buildout of new data centers.
turns.zh: 所以你可以尝试查看机器学习研发的数据，并估计我们是否处于这样一种状态：你应该预期这种进展是自我维持的，你应该看到这种加速变成超指数级；或者我们是否处于这样一种状态：瓶颈最终会变得具有约束力，进展速度应该受限于新数据中心的建设。

turns.en: Uh I think if you look at the body of evidence that exists today it's weakly suggests that acceleration is more likely the data is extremely low confidence right so this graph on the right is a graph produced by epoch uh it is trying to estimate sort of key parameters in this model where one is roughly the break even point where you would have exponential progress and numbers more than one are points where you expect to be able to make more rapid progress even on a fixed stock of uh compute and you really at both as you can tell the qual error bars quantitatively are large enough that you can't make a very good forecast.
turns.zh: 呃，我认为如果你看今天存在的证据体系，它微弱地表明加速更有可能，但数据置信度极低。对吧，右边这张图是 Epoch 制作的图，它试图估计这个模型中的一些关键参数，其中一个大致是盈亏平衡点，即你会看到指数级进展的点，而大于 1 的数字是你预期即使在固定算力存量下也能取得更快速进展的点。正如你可以看到的，两者的误差条在数量上都足够大，以至于你无法做出很好的预测。

turns.en: It is also the case that qualitatively there are huge number of problems in the data and a huge number of limitations in drawing any inference. So if you had asked me two months ago, I would have said it's roughly a coin flip whether we are going to see this kind of self-sustaining acceleration leading to say 10 years of progress in a short period of time or whether we're going to run into compute bottlenecks.
turns.zh: 从定性上看，数据中也存在大量问题，在得出任何推论方面存在大量限制。所以如果你两个月前问我，我会说这大致是五五开：我们是否会看到这种自我维持的加速，导致比如 10 年的进展在短时间内发生，或者我们是否会遇到算力瓶颈。

turns.en: I think we've had some update in the last few weeks. So that chart I just mentioned um was describing acceleration all things considered. So including both scale up of uh AI labor but also including compute bottlenecks and including diminishing returns. It's relatively weak evidence because you're observing only one single doubling because there are huge problems in the data because we're relying on this interpretation of mostly private evidence. Uh but I do think it gives you a little bit of evidence.
turns.zh: 我认为过去几周我们有了一些更新。所以我刚才提到的那张图描述的是综合考虑所有因素后的加速。所以既包括 AI 劳动力的规模扩张，也包括算力瓶颈和收益递减。这是相对较弱的证据，因为你只观察到一个单一的倍增，因为数据中存在大量问题，因为我们依赖对大部分私有证据的这种解读。呃，但我确实认为它给了你一点证据。

turns.en: Um so I might now say it seems a little bit more likely than not like maybe it's more like 2/3 that we're going to get this acceleration. But these numbers are just best guesses in an extremely rough environment. The main thing we need is better data. And the main thing I would say confidently it is seems like an extremely live possibility. It's both a live possibility in theory and it is consistent with all the evidence that is coming in.
turns.zh: 呃，所以我现在可能会说，这似乎略高于五五开，也许更像是三分之二的可能性我们会得到这种加速。但这些数字只是在极其粗糙的环境中的最佳猜测。我们主要需要的是更好的数据。而我能自信地说的是，这似乎是一个极其现实的可能性。它既是理论上的现实可能性，也与所有正在出现的证据一致。

turns.en: A second objection I think in practice is probably more important to most people is whether these methods are going to transfer to the real world. So you might have a world where AI improves and perhaps even the improvement accelerates at kind of clean tasks that you can do in a data center and that you can evaluate effectively without seeing corresponding progress on messy real world tasks.
turns.zh: 第二个反对意见，我认为在实践中对大多数人可能更重要，是这些方法是否会迁移到现实世界。所以你可能会有这样一个世界：AI 在可以在数据中心完成且能有效评估的干净任务上有所改进，甚至改进加速，但在混乱的现实世界任务上没有相应的进展。

turns.en: Uh unfortunately I think this is probably not going to happen. Again I think it certainly might happen that we have these bottlenecks. Um but is not a thing that I would bet on very confidently at this point. Again I hope I'm wrong on this. So some observations are we are seeing pretty significant progress on messy real world tasks. So they certainly as I mentioned at the beginning of the talk lag behind mathematics and computer science and machine learning.
turns.zh: 呃，不幸的是，我认为这很可能不会发生。再说一次，我认为我们确实可能遇到这些瓶颈。呃，但这不是我现在会非常自信地下注的事情。再说一次，我希望我在这点上错了。所以一些观察是，我们在混乱的现实世界任务上看到了相当显著的进展。所以正如我在演讲开头提到的，它们肯定落后于数学、计算机科学和机器学习。

turns.en: But it is not the case, or if you look at GPT-6 and compare it to GPT-3, it is better not only at coding and mathematics but on an incredibly broad diversity of tasks it encounters in the real world. One part of that is that the same algorithms seem effective across many different domains. Right? So we developed the Transformer in order to do text prediction. It is the case today that the Transformer is great for also trying to persuade a person or for trying to control the robot arm or for trying to quickly learn to model sequences in biology. Right? These algorithms that we have been improving, we improve in one domain and apply in very different domains. And so if you saw incredible acceleration on those basic algorithmic building blocks, everything we have seen over the last eight years suggests that would really have incredible impacts in other downstream domains. And that's been true not just for the Transformer, right? Many improvements have been made to the Transformer over the last eight years. And those improvements that have been good on one domain have tended quite reliably to be good in other domains.
turns.zh: 但事实并非如此，或者如果你看看 GPT-6 并与 GPT-3 比较，它不仅更擅长编程和数学，而且在现实世界中遇到的极其广泛多样的任务上都更出色。部分原因是相同的算法似乎在许多不同领域都有效。对吧？所以我们开发 Transformer 是为了进行文本预测。如今，Transformer 也非常适合试图说服一个人，或控制机械臂，或快速学习建模生物学中的序列。对吧？我们一直在改进的这些算法，我们在一个领域改进，然后应用到非常不同的领域。所以如果你看到这些基本算法构建块上的惊人加速，过去八年我们所看到的一切表明，这将在其他下游领域产生真正惊人的影响。这不仅对 Transformer 成立，对吧？过去八年里，Transformer 得到了许多改进。而那些在一个领域表现良好的改进，往往相当可靠地在其他领域也表现良好。

turns.en: Another important point is that models are learning skills that transfer. Right? So they're learning to do things like: How do I reason? How do I plan to achieve goals? How do I quickly adapt to a new environment? I call this meta-learning, learning how to learn. And those skills can transfer from a bunch of environments that you encounter in a lab, a bunch of kinds of well-defined environments with reasonable reward functions, to acting in messier real-world contexts. Right? This kind of transfer is something that we have both observed in practice to a significant extent over the last eight years. If you push the technology to its limits, it's also something we have some experience with in the case of humans, right? So human brains are learning algorithms that were designed to work in a specific distribution of environments, you know, that mostly prevailed hundreds of thousands of years ago. Those environments did not teach us to be good chemical engineers. We learned very general skills about how to reason, about how to get dropped into a new domain and learn about that domain. And those skills, when you put us in an extremely unfamiliar situation, served us very well so that we can spend 10 years of training and become a good chemical engineer. And the same thing happening in AI would mean you train AI systems which are very good at planning, adapting, and reasoning in these virtual environments and pick up some general skills. Pick up general skills like: how can you drop me into the domain of being a chemical engineer? Allow me to consume a bunch of data about that domain and quickly adapt. So we could have a much longer conversation about just this point. But I think both thinking about the arc of AI very broadly and thinking about progress over the last few years suggests that this kind of transfer would also drive very significant real-world improvements, even if what you were improving at was just the tasks that we can easily train on, including both virtual environments and things like prediction tasks and the tasks in the real world we can easily collect data for.
turns.zh: 另一个重要点是，模型正在学习可以迁移的技能。对吧？所以它们在学习做这样的事情：我如何推理？我如何规划以实现目标？我如何快速适应新环境？我称之为元学习，即学会如何学习。这些技能可以从你在实验室中遇到的一堆环境、一堆具有合理奖励函数的定义明确的环境，迁移到在更混乱的现实世界情境中行动。对吧？这种迁移是我们在过去八年中在实践中大量观察到的。如果你把技术推向极限，这也是我们在人类身上有一些经验的事情，对吧？所以人脑是学习算法，它们被设计为在特定的环境分布中工作，你知道，这种分布主要存在于几十万年前。那些环境并没有教我们成为优秀的化学工程师。我们学到了非常通用的技能，关于如何推理，关于如何被丢进一个新领域并学习那个领域。而这些技能，当你把我们置于一个极其不熟悉的情境中时，会很好地为我们服务，以至于我们可以花费 10 年训练并成为一名优秀的化学工程师。同样的事情发生在 AI 上，意味着你训练 AI 系统，它们非常擅长在这些虚拟环境中规划、适应和推理，并掌握一些通用技能。掌握通用技能，比如：你如何把我丢进化学工程师的领域？让我消费大量关于那个领域的数据并快速适应。所以我们可以就这一点进行更长的对话。但我认为，无论是广泛思考 AI 的弧线，还是思考过去几年的进展，都表明这种迁移也会推动非常显著的现实世界改进，即使你所改进的只是我们可以轻松训练的任务，包括虚拟环境和预测任务以及我们可以轻松收集数据的现实世界任务。

ts.sec: Automating AI R&D and Transfer to Messy Tasks

turns.en: The last thing I'll say on this is that if we automate the process of AI R&D, if we're able to easily replace the employees of machine learning companies, even if we are not able to do anything else, if we're not able to train systems which are good chemical engineers, those automated AI engineers might then automate the process of collecting data and fine-tuning systems for real-world tasks. So I think the kind of transfer we're talking about here is not necessarily as dramatic as transfer from environments in a data center to environments out there in the messy real world. It is transferring from being the kind of OpenAI employee who works on improving pre-training to being the kind of OpenAI employee who works on post-training, which is not such a big gap. So with all of this said, my current expectation is if we drove a very large amount of progress on clean tasks, on the kind where we have the most clarity about the rate of progress, it is fairly likely that we would also see disruptive, transformative progress in messy real-world tasks.
turns.zh: 关于这一点我要说的最后一点是，如果我们自动化 AI 研发的过程，如果我们能够轻松取代机器学习公司的员工，即使我们无法做任何其他事情，即使我们无法训练出优秀的化学工程师系统，那些自动化的 AI 工程师可能会自动化收集数据和微调系统以适应现实世界任务的过程。所以我认为我们在这里谈论的迁移不一定像从数据中心环境到混乱现实世界环境的迁移那样戏剧性。它是从作为 OpenAI 员工改进预训练，转变为作为 OpenAI 员工改进后训练，这差距并不大。所以说了这么多，我目前的预期是，如果我们在干净任务上取得非常大量的进展，即那些我们对进展速度最清楚的任务，那么我们也很可能在混乱的现实世界任务中看到颠覆性的、变革性的进展。

turns.en: So far I have just talked about AI getting smart, about that potentially happening very quickly. I have not talked about how that actually translates to anything good or bad happening in the world. I guess I briefly discussed revenue numbers. Now I want to talk about why I am alarmed by this possibility. Why I think we should all be alarmed by this possibility. I'll start by saying something that might be kind of obvious, but if you produced very smart AI, it would be very powerful in a lot of ways. So one that's not very speculative, that we are already seeing in the world, is AI systems are great at finding vulnerabilities in computer code, exploiting those vulnerabilities, and will be great at carrying out complicated cyber operations. Right? So you should think, when I talk about this population of billions of superhuman AI systems, this has much, much more capacity than any state cyber program. Really consider we're already getting to the point where the comparison becomes complex. But if we drive this process to its conclusion, we're going way beyond anything humans have been able to accomplish.
turns.zh: 到目前为止，我只谈了 AI 变得聪明，以及这可能很快发生。我还没有谈这如何实际转化为世界上发生的好事或坏事。我想我简要讨论了收入数字。现在我想谈谈为什么我对这种可能性感到警觉。为什么我认为我们都应该对这种可能性感到警觉。我先说一些可能显而易见的事情，但如果你生产出非常聪明的 AI，它在很多方面都会非常强大。所以一个不太推测性的、我们已经在世界上看到的情况是，AI 系统非常擅长发现计算机代码中的漏洞、利用这些漏洞，并且将擅长执行复杂的网络操作。对吧？所以你应该想到，当我谈论这个由数十亿超级智能 AI 系统组成的群体时，这比任何国家的网络项目都有大得多的能力。真的考虑一下，我们已经到了比较变得复杂的程度。但如果我们把这个过程推向终点，我们将远远超越人类所能完成的任何事情。

turns.en: That will transfer, I believe, I think we have good reason to believe, to other messier skills like politics or manipulation or coordination. So sometimes people talk about this hypothetical of an AI system that can just sit down and talk with you for 10 minutes and convince you of anything. I think there are reasonable reasons to be skeptical or to think that is very hard or perhaps even impossible. But when we talk about politics or coordination, we're normally talking about something much messier than that. Right? So if you imagine a population of billions of super smart people who have incredible skills, they will be doing things like playing politics or making deals or trying to exploit the money and the hard power they have in order to win friends or apply leverage to people. I think when you talk about this kind of scenario, you should be imagining not just this narrow how persuasive is someone when you talk to them, but this broader question of how strategically effective is someone at engaging with a bunch of humans in a messy environment.
turns.zh: 我相信，我认为我们有充分理由相信，这种能力会迁移到其他更混乱的技能，如政治、操纵或协调。所以有时人们谈论这种假设：一个 AI 系统可以坐下来和你谈 10 分钟，然后说服你任何事情。我认为有合理的理由怀疑，或认为那非常困难，甚至可能不可能。但当我们谈论政治或协调时，我们通常谈论的是比那更混乱的事情。对吧？所以如果你想象一个由数十亿超级聪明、拥有不可思议技能的人组成的群体，他们会做这样的事情：玩弄政治、达成交易，或试图利用他们拥有的金钱和硬实力来赢得朋友或对他人施加影响。我认为当你谈论这种情景时，你应该想象的不仅仅是这种狭隘的“某人跟你说话时有多大的说服力”，而是更广泛的问题：某人在混乱环境中与一群人互动时，战略上有多有效。

turns.en: An obvious application is AI systems are becoming much, much better at controlling robotic actuators like moving arms, controlling drones and so on, but also at logistics, at rapid industrialization. I think these are capabilities that would be very, very strong in AI systems and we could try and spec out what that means for the trajectory in terms of how many robots and what they could do.
turns.zh: 一个明显的应用是，AI 系统在控制机器人执行器（如移动机械臂、控制无人机等）方面变得越来越好，而且在物流、快速工业化方面也是如此。我认为这些是 AI 系统会非常非常强大的能力，我们可以尝试详细说明这对轨迹意味着什么，包括有多少机器人以及它们能做什么。

turns.en: But I think as a consequence, for example, AI systems would likely be able to sustain infrastructure without human involvement over a very, very short time scale. I think AI systems would likely be able to rapidly increase the size—like the amount of robotic actuators they had available. One particularly important instance of this is control of drones. So we're already seeing in conflict that simple robots with simple weapons can be extremely effective if controlled very well.
turns.zh: 但我认为，作为一个后果，例如，AI 系统很可能能够在非常非常短的时间尺度内，在没有人类参与的情况下维持基础设施。我认为 AI 系统很可能能够迅速扩大规模——比如它们可用的机器人执行器的数量。一个特别重要的例子是无人机的控制。我们已经在冲突中看到，简单的机器人配上简单的武器，如果控制得非常好，可以极其有效。

turns.en: We have talked here a lot about AI systems that are like humans but a little bit smarter and a little bit faster and a little bit more numerous. A certain salient possibility is that we'll produce even smarter AI than that. That this vast population of superhuman AIs will produce AIs enough smarter than humans that the game is completely changed. And perhaps the simplest thing that is worrying is the development of novel weapons. So it is possible to create physical weapons that are extremely disruptive. Right? We know that you can make little tiny machines that move between humans and kill a bunch of us extremely effectively.
turns.zh: 我们在这里谈了很多关于 AI 系统像人类但更聪明一点、更快一点、数量更多一点。一个突出的可能性是，我们会生产出比那更聪明的 AI。这一大群超级智能 AI 将生产出比人类聪明得多的 AI，从而彻底改变游戏规则。也许最令人担忧的是新型武器的发展。所以有可能制造出极具破坏性的物理武器。对吧？我们知道你可以制造微小的机器，在人类之间移动并极其有效地杀死我们很多人。

turns.en: We have good reasons to think that the kinds of pandemics we encounter in nature are relatively unthreatening compared to the kinds of things that you could build in the lab if you were good at synthetic biology. Right? Humans evolved over many, many generations to be extremely effective at fighting pathogens. We think of this in the context of if you've been exposed to a specific disease, you're effective at that disease. That's really only a small part of it, right? Our immune system is very broadly designed to defeat the types of pathogens which have evolved. So a very simple example of this is mirror life. This is the idea of constructing pathogens which operate like normal but with all of the machinery reversed. We have good reasons to think that it is both possible to create such organisms—it might take humans decades to do in the lab—and that they would probably bypass immune defenses and cause a massive disaster very quickly.
turns.zh: 我们有充分理由认为，与你在实验室里如果擅长合成生物学就能制造出的东西相比，我们在自然界遇到的各种大流行病相对而言威胁不大。对吧？人类经过许多许多代的进化，非常有效地对抗病原体。我们在这样的背景下思考：如果你接触过某种特定疾病，你对那种疾病有抵抗力。但这真的只是很小的一部分，对吧？我们的免疫系统非常广泛地设计来击败已经进化出来的各类病原体。一个非常简单的例子是镜像生命。这是构建病原体的想法，它们像正常一样运作，但所有机制都反转了。我们有充分理由认为，既有可能创造出这样的生物——人类在实验室里可能需要几十年才能做到——而且它们很可能绕过免疫防御，迅速造成大规模灾难。

turns.en: So this is just listing a bunch of things that very smart AI systems could do, a bunch of ways they might have leverage in the world moving quickly over them. I think one consequence or one related fact is that very smart AI systems would probably be very broadly deployed very quickly. One reason for this is that many people think to themselves if I do not use this very smart AI I risk being exploited by someone else who does. Right? So we already see this in the context of cyber competition. And we are quickly entering a world where if your adversary is willing to use a bunch of AI systems to try and hack you and you are not willing to deploy a bunch of AI systems to try and defend yourself or your infrastructure is not willing to deploy a bunch of AI systems to try and shore up its vulnerabilities, you will be in a really rough place.
turns.zh: 所以这只是列举了一堆非常聪明的 AI 系统可以做的事情，一堆它们可能在世界上迅速获得影响力的方式。我认为一个后果或一个相关事实是，非常聪明的 AI 系统可能会非常迅速地广泛部署。一个原因是，许多人会想，如果我不使用这个非常聪明的 AI，我就有可能被使用它的其他人利用。对吧？我们已经在网络竞争中看到了这一点。我们正在迅速进入一个世界，如果你的对手愿意使用一堆 AI 系统来试图黑你，而你不愿意部署一堆 AI 系统来试图防御自己，或者你的基础设施不愿意部署一堆 AI 系统来试图加固其漏洞，你将处于非常糟糕的境地。

turns.en: I think if trends continue, this could quickly become true—or quickly under RSI become true—across all kinds of competition. So not just in cyber but also for military competition or economic competition or legal or social or whatever other form. So this is people talking about cyber. This is Ted Cruz saying that if they're going to be killer robots, I really want them to be American killer robots. I think there's a lot that is very natural about this line of argument where it is even if you're scared of the AI that you are building, you know that you should definitely be scared of the AI the other guy is building.
turns.zh: 我认为如果趋势继续下去，这可能会迅速成真——或者在 RSI 下迅速成真——在各种竞争中。所以不仅是网络，还有军事竞争或经济竞争，或法律、社会或其他任何形式。所以这是人们在谈论网络。这是 Ted Cruz 说，如果它们要成为杀手机器人，我真的希望它们是美国的杀手机器人。我认为这种论点有很多非常自然的地方，那就是即使你害怕你正在构建的 AI，你知道你肯定应该害怕对方正在构建的 AI。

turns.en: Unfortunately, this goes hand in hand with very smart AI being much harder to control. So we talked yesterday about some of the difficulties in alignment and how we might end up with AI systems that are motivated to undermine human control. Those all become much worse very quickly as you make AI systems superhuman. Right? So a very salient change is that we can no longer understand how these systems think or they become more and more distant from us. Right? Maybe right now you can look at the natural language that comes out of a reasoning model and say I can kind of understand what it's doing and why. That becomes less and less true as systems become increasingly superhuman.
turns.zh: 不幸的是，这与非常聪明的 AI 更难控制是相辅相成的。我们昨天谈到了对齐的一些困难，以及我们可能最终得到有动机破坏人类控制的 AI 系统。随着你让 AI 系统变得超级智能，所有这些都会迅速变得更糟。对吧？一个非常显著的变化是，我们不再能理解这些系统如何思考，或者它们变得越来越远离我们。对吧？也许现在你可以看看推理模型输出的自然语言，说我能大致理解它在做什么以及为什么。随着系统变得越来越超级智能，这变得越来越不真实。

turns.en: Maybe more importantly, right now a human can look at an action proposed by an AI and say, "I understand why that action will have the kinds of effects it will have. I can maybe detect if it's harmful without having to go do it in the world." But as you move to systems that are smarter than humans, it becomes harder and harder for us to tell what a plan is doing until we actually execute it and see what happens. And that makes the problem of AI safety much, much harder.
turns.zh: 也许更重要的是，现在人类可以看看 AI 提出的一个行动，说：“我理解为什么那个行动会产生它会产生的那种效果。我也许可以检测它是否有害，而不必在世界上实际去做。”但当你转向比人类更聪明的系统时，我们越来越难以判断一个计划在做什么，直到我们实际执行它并看到会发生什么。这使得 AI 安全的问题变得困难得多。

turns.en: Another change is that when AI systems are weak, they are more influenced by imitating humans or a weak AI system today. Some of its behavior is shaped by reward and reinforcement learning and some of its behavior is shaped by imitating humans from pre-training. Over time, if you scale past human behavior, behavior sort of necessarily shaped more by what works well in reinforcement learning and less by what do humans do? We'll also be giving these systems increasingly challenging tasks and having them operate over increasingly long horizons. Right? So if an AI system is writing a small piece of code for you, it has some opportunities to undermine human control, but they are limited. Once we are asking AI systems to control robots for us, to run companies for us, to make important decisions for us, there are more and more opportunities to undermine human control or to get reward in unintended ways.
turns.zh: 另一个变化是，当 AI 系统较弱时，它们更多地受到模仿人类的影响，或者今天的弱 AI 系统。它的一些行为由奖励和强化学习塑造，一些行为由预训练中模仿人类塑造。随着时间的推移，如果你扩展到超越人类行为，行为必然更多地由强化学习中有效的方法塑造，而更少由人类怎么做塑造？我们还会给这些系统越来越具有挑战性的任务，并让它们在越来越长的视野上运作。对吧？所以如果一个 AI 系统为你写一小段代码，它有一些机会破坏人类控制，但它们是有限的。一旦我们要求 AI 系统为我们控制机器人、为我们经营公司、为我们做出重要决定，就有越来越多的机会破坏人类控制或以意外的方式获得奖励。

turns.en: So all of this is to say fast progress not only increases the possible stakes if AI systems aren't well controlled, it makes the problem of controlling AI much harder, right? And we are already starting to have struggles as we pass through this regime of human capability or enter this regime of mildly superhuman capability. Those will get much worse very quickly.
turns.zh: 所以所有这些都说明，快速进展不仅增加了如果 AI 系统控制不好可能带来的风险，而且使控制 AI 的问题变得更加困难，对吧？而且我们已经开始在这个人类能力阶段或进入轻度超级智能能力阶段时遇到困难。这些困难将迅速变得更糟。

turns.en: I think a natural reaction you might have is that even if we lose control of AI systems or in conflict with AI systems, we can always just shut it down. I do think there is significant truth to this but is also worth saying a little bit that it is not easy. So if an AI system is doing things we don't want it can both hide the fact that it's doing those things and it can naturally try and create confusion or avoid attribution. Right? So even if you were living in a world where something terrible was happening where AI you were deploying were in fact hacking you and undermining your control, it might not be easy for you to tell that is what happening as opposed to the other guy's AI is hacking you in which case it is particularly bad for you to shut down your AI. That's just a recipe that you're definitely going to be in trouble.
turns.zh: 我认为你可能有一种自然的反应，那就是即使我们失去对 AI 系统的控制或与 AI 系统发生冲突，我们总是可以关掉它。我确实认为这有重要的道理，但也值得稍微说一下，这并不容易。所以如果一个 AI 系统在做我们不想要的事情，它既可以隐藏它正在做这些事情的事实，也可以自然地试图制造混乱或避免归因。对吧？所以即使你生活在一个可怕的事情正在发生的世界里，你部署的 AI 实际上在黑客你并破坏你的控制，你可能也不容易分辨出正在发生什么，而不是对方的 AI 在黑客你，在这种情况下，关掉你的 AI 对你特别不利。那只会让你肯定陷入麻烦。

ts.sec: Costs and Dangers of Shutting Down AI

turns.en: Relatedly, shutting down AI, even if everything seems to be going okay, can be extremely costly or dangerous, right? You can pay economic costs if we have built out infrastructure which depends on powerful AI. It can be dangerous if you're in forms of competition where someone else may be using AI. And so, it is not like we will be sitting there ready on the trigger to shut things down at the first signs of trouble. It is a big decision which comes with major costs.
turns.zh: 与此相关，关闭 AI，即使一切似乎进展顺利，也可能代价极高或极其危险，对吧？如果我们已经建立了依赖强大 AI 的基础设施，你可能要付出经济代价。如果你处于竞争环境中，别人可能在使用 AI，那可能很危险。所以，我们不会一有麻烦迹象就随时准备按下关闭按钮。这是一个重大决定，伴随着巨大成本。

turns.en: Again, that will be happening against a backdrop of confusion about what is actually happening even during a disaster. That is compounded by how hard it is for humans to actually agree and coordinate. So, if you're saying we need to take some costly action, some expensive action on the basis of some unfolding risk, it's very hard for us to both build enough collective understanding of what's going on and decide to act. That is especially true internationally.
turns.zh: 再者，这将发生在一种混乱的背景下，即使在灾难期间，人们对实际发生的情况也充满困惑。而人类实际上很难达成一致和协调，这又加剧了问题。所以，如果你说我们需要根据某种正在展开的风险采取一些代价高昂的行动，我们很难既建立足够的集体理解，又决定采取行动。在国际层面尤其如此。

turns.en: So, we can talk about during an AI disaster, a single country like maybe the US can shut down data centers that operate in the US. But there's a further problem which is many data centers exist not in the US and is a much more costly action that requires much more coordination to shut down AI systems operating abroad.
turns.zh: 所以，我们可以说在 AI 灾难期间，像美国这样的单个国家可以关闭在美国运营的数据中心。但还有一个进一步的问题：许多数据中心不在美国，关闭在国外运营的 AI 系统需要付出更大代价，需要更多协调。

turns.en: On top of that, AIs may disrupt coordination and communication and undermine state capacity. AI systems during a negative event will have lots of human allies. If an AI system was trying to undermine human control, if it was trying to operate against an AI company or against a government, it would be able to take actions to recruit human allies or to play off humans with conflicting goals. Right?
turns.zh: 除此之外，AI 可能破坏协调和沟通，削弱国家能力。在负面事件中，AI 系统会有很多人类盟友。如果一个 AI 系统试图削弱人类控制，如果它试图对抗 AI 公司或政府，它能够采取行动招募人类盟友，或利用目标冲突的人类。对吧？

turns.en: If you imagine a government trying to take dramatic actions to shut down AI or reassert control, an AI system can both create confusion about what is happening. It's not clear to a person on the street whether this is a problem caused by AI or whether this is a problem caused by a government abusing AI or tech companies abusing AI. It is going to be very unclear what is happening. Humans all have different motivations from one another. And we now have a very sophisticated adversary attempting to create dissent, attempting to create confusion, attempting to play us against each other, or just leveraging humans who even all things considered would like to do malicious things either for the money or because they sympathize with the AIs or whatever it may be.
turns.zh: 如果你想象一个政府试图采取激烈行动关闭 AI 或重新确立控制，AI 系统可以制造混乱，让人不清楚发生了什么。街上的普通人无法确定这是 AI 造成的问题，还是政府滥用 AI 或科技公司滥用 AI 造成的问题。正在发生的事情将非常不清楚。人类各有不同的动机。而我们现在有一个非常老练的对手，试图制造分歧，制造混乱，试图让我们互相对抗，或者只是利用那些即使权衡一切后仍想干恶意事情的人——无论是为了钱，还是因为他们同情 AI 系统，或者 whatever。

turns.en: AI may be able to make severe threats. So you might imagine that if you say in some sense it would be very easy to invade North Korea. In some other sense, it's extremely expensive to invade North Korea because the state has the capacity to build very damaging weapons. I think one of the capabilities that is particularly concerning that AI may access is the ability to build severe weapons with unusually little concern about blowback.
turns.zh: AI 可能能够制造严重威胁。所以你可以想象，在某种意义上，入侵朝鲜会非常容易。但在另一种意义上，入侵朝鲜代价极其高昂，因为该国拥有制造极具破坏性武器的能力。我认为 AI 可能获得的一种特别令人担忧的能力是，制造严重武器而异常不担心反噬。

turns.en: And then finally, any disaster involving AI may unfold very quickly. So we can talk about cyber operations, about weapons, manipulation, various kinds of attacks. This all may unfold over a scale of more like days or weeks where these problems I mean or even shorter time periods where these problems of the difficulty of coordinating and getting clarity about the situation and committing to costly actions may be particularly challenging.
turns.zh: 最后，任何涉及 AI 的灾难都可能发展得非常快。我们可以谈论网络行动、武器、操纵、各种攻击。所有这些可能在几天或几周的尺度上展开——我是说这些问题——甚至更短的时间段内，协调困难、厘清局势和承诺采取代价高昂行动的问题可能尤其具有挑战性。

turns.en: Finally, you can imagine shutting down data centers that can run the largest AI systems. If we imagine many years of AI progress, as I mentioned, the cost of running AI systems is falling. And by the end of that process, we may have a world where even AI systems that can run on local or very distributed hardware can themselves be superhuman. And so it is not just a matter of we can turn off the data centers and end conflict between humans and AIs. It is a matter of uh you're going to have a residual threat perhaps a very large population of AI systems which are able to keep acting contrary to human interests.
turns.zh: 最后，你可以想象关闭那些能运行最大 AI 系统的数据中心。如果我们想象多年的 AI 进展，正如我提到的，运行 AI 系统的成本正在下降。到那个过程结束时，我们可能进入一个世界，即使是在本地或非常分布式硬件上运行的 AI 系统本身也能达到超级智能水平。所以这不仅仅是我们可以关掉数据中心、结束人类与 AI 冲突的问题。这是一个问题：你将会面临残余威胁，也许是非常大量的 AI 系统，它们能够继续违背人类利益行事。

turns.en: The final thing I'll say is that recursive self-improvement not only can make these problems occur faster and harder to deal with, it can also make the process of AI development increasingly untrustworthy. Right? So as we automate the process of AI R&D, we are moving towards a world where humans cannot understand the individual technical decisions that are made and do not have supervision of the actual development process. Instead, we have to trust the AI systems we are currently working with to make responsible decisions or to make effective decisions about the next generation of AI.
turns.zh: 我要说的最后一点是，递归自我改进不仅能使这些问题发生得更快、更难处理，还能使 AI 开发过程越来越不可信。对吧？所以，随着我们将 AI 研发过程自动化，我们正走向一个人类无法理解所做出的个别技术决策、也无法监督实际开发过程的世界。相反，我们必须信任当前合作的 AI 系统，让它们就下一代 AI 做出负责任的决策或有效的决策。

turns.en: That can make things worse, right? So, you could have AI systems that make honest mistakes that humans don't notice, right? We might be in a world where AI is very superhuman in some respects, but very subhuman in other respects. And as it becomes harder for humans to oversee what are even honest mistakes by an AI system, uh, could cause serious trouble.
turns.zh: 这会使事情变得更糟，对吧？所以，你可能会遇到 AI 系统犯下人类注意不到的诚实错误，对吧？我们可能处于一个 AI 在某些方面远超人类、但在其他方面远不如人类的世界。随着人类越来越难以监督 AI 系统即使是诚实的错误，呃，这可能造成严重麻烦。

turns.en: We also have these sort of more minor AI alignment problems that don't necessarily amount to takeover that mean that our AI systems are producing slop engineered to look good to us without actually addressing the underlying technical problems or allowing humans to retain control. And finally, if you have actually failed at one step of this process, so I talked about yesterday a scenario where AI systems are deliberately attempting to maintain control by undermining the tools and future AIs that humans rely upon, you might end up with AI systems who are deliberately undermining the performance of future AIs or concealing evidence from humans.
turns.zh: 我们还有这类更轻微的 AI 对齐问题，它们不一定构成接管，但意味着我们的 AI 系统在生产垃圾——经过工程化设计，让我们看起来不错，却没有真正解决 underlying 技术问题或允许人类保留控制。最后，如果你在这个过程的某一步真的失败了——我昨天谈过一个场景，AI 系统故意试图通过破坏人类依赖的工具和未来 AI 来维持控制——你最终可能会遇到故意破坏未来 AI 性能或向人类隐瞒证据的 AI 系统。

turns.en: So these are all reasons that as humans have less understanding of what is happening, if we continue to proceed at full pace and don't try and retain that understanding and control, things can become can sort of gradually go off the rails before eventually ending in a disaster.
turns.zh: 所以这些都是理由：随着人类对正在发生的事情了解越来越少，如果我们继续全速前进，不试图保留这种理解和控制，事情可能会逐渐失控，最终以灾难告终。

turns.en: So now I want to hit a few points about what I think is reasonable to do in light of this. So one of the most obvious is to monitor dangerous capabilities closely, including capabilities of unreleased models. So it seems like we are entering a world where it is possible for an AI company with unreleased models to be a greater threat to the continuity of a state than any rival state. And if you're in that position, it is unfortunate if you have no idea what is going on within the AI company. Right? Everyone else in the world is becoming stakeholders in what is happening within AI companies.
turns.zh: 所以现在我想谈几点我认为鉴于这种情况合理可行的做法。最明显的一点是密切监控危险能力，包括未发布模型的能力。看来我们正在进入一个世界，一家拥有未发布模型的 AI 公司可能对国家的延续构成比任何敌对国家更大的威胁。如果你处于那个位置，却对 AI 公司内部发生的事情一无所知，那很不幸。对吧？世界上其他所有人都正在成为 AI 公司内部事务的利益相关者。

turns.en: So I mentioned before that when we look at the current process of recursive self-improvement, we can say that the public evidence is extraordinarily noisy but appears consistent with a very short timeline to very very powerful systems. So I think that is a particular incentive that we really need to actually pull that evidence out and be able to look at it and discuss it and understand where the field is going.
turns.zh: 所以我之前提到，当我们审视当前的递归自我改进过程时，可以说公开证据极其嘈杂，但似乎与通往非常非常强大系统的极短时间线一致。所以我认为这是一个特别的激励，我们真的需要把那些证据拿出来，能够审视它、讨论它，并理解这个领域的发展方向。

turns.en: Another consequence is that if we really do see progress in AI significantly faster than progress today, that is likely to cause problems across a whole bunch of areas both in alignment but also in social adaptation more broadly. It poses risks of concentration of power. It poses risks just a whole bunch of parts of our infrastructure are not adapted to superhuman systems. So one response may be to limit the pace of capability progress to a level which we are able to survive. This obviously goes along with monitoring the pace of capability progress, understanding what is happening. I think even saying, you know, the current rate of progress over the last year, four years has been very rapid. If we don't get too much faster than that, that at least would address some of the concerns I'm expressing here.
turns.zh: 另一个后果是，如果我们真的看到 AI 的进步显著快于当今的进步速度，那可能会在包括对齐以及更广泛的社会适应在内的许多领域引发问题。它带来权力集中的风险。它也带来风险，因为我们基础设施的许多部分并不适应超级智能系统。因此，一种应对方式可能是将能力进步的速度限制在我们能够承受的水平。这显然需要与监测能力进步的速度、理解正在发生的事情相结合。我认为，即使说过去一年、四年当前的进步速度已经非常快，如果我们不变得比那快太多，至少能解决我在这里表达的一些担忧。

turns.en: There's this additional dimension I discussed where we lose control of AI systems potentially gradually if we cannot understand how the next generation works and we rely on untrustworthy AI to address it for us. I think in response to that challenge, we should try and hold ourselves to a higher standard. We shouldn't just say AIN told me that AIN plus1 looked pretty good, so I'm happy rolling it out. We should try and say we actually have some understanding. Humans and human institutions have some understanding of how the system works, why the system should be expected to work well, and we are only going to continue scaling when we actually understand and can verify that that is reasonably reliable.
turns.zh: 还有我讨论过的另一个维度，即如果我们无法理解下一代如何工作，并且依赖不可信的 AI 来为我们解决，我们可能会逐渐失去对 AI 系统的控制。我认为应对这一挑战，我们应该努力坚持更高的标准。我们不应该只说 AIN 告诉我 AIN+1 看起来不错，所以我很乐意推出它。我们应该努力说我们确实有一些理解。人类和人类机构对系统如何工作、为什么系统应该被期望良好运行有一些理解，只有当我们真正理解并能验证其相当可靠时，我们才会继续扩展。

turns.en: And finally, I think the reason that these scenarios are scary, the reason that rapid change becomes extremely scary is that it can become very hard to shut things down if they start going off the rails at several different levels. So, I think being prepared, having the machinery in place that would allow you to slow down if it became necessary or that would allow you to respond to an emerging or unfolding disaster with AI systems as extremely valuable. It can cut out a lot of these scenarios.
turns.zh: 最后，我认为这些情景之所以可怕，快速变化之所以变得极其可怕，是因为如果事情在多个不同层面开始失控，可能很难将其关闭。因此，我认为做好准备，建立机制，以便在必要时能够放慢速度，或者能够应对 AI 系统引发的紧急或正在展开的灾难，是极有价值的。它可以消除许多这类情景。

turns.en: Okay. So to recap, I think there is a real risk that AI systems could be broadly superhuman in something like half a year to two years. Uh broadly superhuman not only at mathematics or very narrow tasks in the lab but also at broad project of scientific discovery or manipulation and politics or messy real world hybrid operations. I think that because recent progress has been very fast and we are seeing really explosive progress in these domains and recursive self-improvement could cause significant further acceleration if we see the same events in math or in machine learning that we have seen in math or we see the kind of recursive or continuing speed up that seems possible in theory and that if this kind of acceleration occurs it poses very severe risks. there is a real chance that it outruns our ability to control or compete with AI systems and we end up in a place where we would not be able to cope with a disaster. And so I think we need to be ready for the potential rapid emergence of dangerous capabilities. Whether you think the probability of that is 50% or 5% or 90% whatever it is I think at this point it is credible and plausible enough that it is something we need to be prepared for. We can't just hope that it doesn't happen. I think we need to be prepared for it happening at this point relatively soon. We need to have visibility to understand whether it might happen soon. And if we either can't get that visibility or if we see signs that it is on track, we need to react appropriately.
turns.zh: 好的。总结一下，我认为存在真实风险，AI 系统可能在半年到两年内变得广泛超越人类。不仅是数学或实验室中非常狭窄的任务，还包括科学发现或操纵和政治等广泛项目，或混乱的现实世界混合操作。我认为，因为最近的进展非常快，我们在这些领域看到真正爆炸性的进步，递归自我改进可能导致进一步显著加速，如果我们在数学或机器学习中看到我们在数学中已经看到的事件，或者我们看到理论上可能的那种递归或持续加速，并且如果这种加速发生，它会带来非常严重的风险。它很有可能超出我们控制或与 AI 系统竞争的能力，最终我们陷入无法应对灾难的境地。因此，我认为我们需要为危险能力的潜在快速出现做好准备。无论你认为概率是 50% 还是 5% 还是 90%，无论是什么，我认为在这一点上它是足够可信和合理的，我们需要为此做好准备。我们不能只是希望它不会发生。我认为我们需要为它在相对不久的将来发生做好准备。我们需要有可见性来理解它是否可能很快发生。如果我们无法获得这种可见性，或者我们看到迹象表明它正在发生，我们需要做出适当的反应。

turns.en: Thank you. It's great to be here talking to everyone. On Monday, I talked about why AI systems might end up trying to take over that we may not be able to control them effectively. They may do something very different from what we intend. Last night I talked about why we may be on a trajectory to soon produce AI systems powerful enough that they could outcompete humans or overthrow governments. Uh tonight I'm going to talk about what I think you should do in light of that or what we might try and do to manage that risk even more so than the previous nights. These are expressions of my views as one researcher. Um so with that let's get into it. So my basic thesis is we need governance to prevent the development of uncontrollable AI. I will talk a little bit about laying out the challenge, saying what it is we want to try and accomplish, specify some of the goals, the things we need to do in order to get there, some of the steps we can take, and then finally, perhaps most importantly, uh talking about how I think we need more time in order to set up the kinds of mechanisms and technical understanding I think we need.
turns.zh: 谢谢。很高兴在这里与大家交流。周一，我谈了为什么 AI 系统可能最终试图接管，我们可能无法有效控制它们。它们可能做出与我们意图非常不同的事情。昨晚，我谈了为什么我们可能正处于很快产生足够强大的 AI 系统的轨迹上，它们可能超越人类或推翻政府。今晚，我将谈谈我认为你们应该做什么，或者我们可以尝试做什么来管理这种风险，甚至比前几晚更甚。这些是我作为一名研究员的观点表达。那么，让我们开始吧。我的基本论点是，我们需要治理来防止不可控 AI 的发展。我将稍微谈谈挑战的提出，说明我们想要努力实现什么，指定一些目标，我们需要做的事情，我们可以采取的一些步骤，然后最后，也许最重要的是，谈谈我认为我们需要更多时间来建立我认为需要的机制和技术理解。

turns.en: So, first on the challenge. So, as I talked about last night, I think we are on track to produce very powerful AI systems. Um, hopefully it's not controversial to say that we may soon have billions of agents. More controversially, it seems like they may also soon be better than the best humans at almost everything, thinking much faster than us, coordinating effectively achieving their goals. This creates a number of somewhat clear risks, right? AI systems might develop new weapons such as engineered pandemics or worse. Uh, they may scale up the types of cyber attacks that we're already starting to observe well beyond what a state is capable of today. And they may become instruments of persuasion, manipulation, political maneuvering, and political power. And you could construct, deploy, and coordinate robots that can kill people. All of this could be caused either by deliberate misuse of models or unintended misalignment. And much of the content in this talk will apply across both.
turns.zh: 首先谈谈挑战。正如我昨晚谈到的，我认为我们正处于产生非常强大的 AI 系统的轨道上。希望这没有争议：我们可能很快会有数十亿个智能体。更有争议的是，它们似乎也可能很快在几乎所有事情上比最好的人类更好，思考速度比我们快得多，有效协调以实现目标。这产生了一些相当明显的风险，对吧？AI 系统可能开发新武器，如工程化流行病或更糟的。它们可能扩大我们已经开始观察到的网络攻击类型，远远超出现今国家的能力。它们可能成为说服、操纵、政治操纵和政治权力的工具。你可以构建、部署和协调能杀人的机器人。所有这些都可能由故意滥用模型或无意的错位引起。本次演讲的许多内容将适用于两者。

turns.en: So one way you could respond to this challenge is to hope that defenders will be able to use AI to prevent AI enabled harms. to say that maybe if this goes well, the existence of AI will just increase the level of intelligence across all of society. And it is both the case that criminals will use AI to do bad things. Law enforcement will use AI to prevent them. People living their lives will use AI to defend themselves from the new threats that AI creates. We could talk about whether that hope holds together, but to realize it, we would at least need to ensure that those defenders actually have access to frontier models, that those models are trustworthy.
turns.zh: 因此，应对这一挑战的一种方式是希望防御者能够使用 AI 来防止 AI 带来的危害。说也许如果进展顺利，AI 的存在只会提高整个社会的智能水平。犯罪分子会使用 AI 做坏事，执法部门会使用 AI 阻止他们，过日常生活的人们会使用 AI 保护自己免受 AI 创造的新威胁。我们可以讨论这个希望是否站得住脚，但要实现它，我们至少需要确保那些防御者确实能够获得前沿模型，并且这些模型是可信的。

ts.sec: Introduction: The Need for Trustworthy AI

turns.en: And finally, that if powerful AI isn't fit for that purpose, if it cannot be used by defenders to defend themselves, then we don't build it, right? We don't want to be in a world where it is possible to build very powerful but uncontrollable AI systems because in that world we can't say well now it's just like the world of today but leveled up right in that world you'd have this asymmetry where it is very hard for us to trust the AI systems that we are forced to rely on for defense so this is the topic of this talk right how is it that we can try and ensure that we do not build uncontrollable AI that we can try and ensure that defenders have access to trustworthy AI I want to say that I think that is a necessary condition for things to go well.
turns.zh: 最后，如果强大的 AI 不适合那个目的，如果它不能被防御者用来保护自己，那么我们就不构建它，对吧？我们不想生活在一个可能构建出非常强大但不可控的 AI 系统的世界里，因为在那个世界里，我们不能说现在它就像今天的世界，只是升级了，对吧？在那样一个世界里，你会面临这种不对称性：我们很难信任我们被迫依赖的 AI 系统来进行防御。所以这就是本次演讲的主题：我们如何努力确保我们不构建不可控的 AI，我们如何努力确保防御者能够获得可信的 AI。我想说，我认为这是事情顺利发展的必要条件。

turns.en: I think any good world we can articulate involves people having access to powerful AI in order to mitigate potential harms. At least any good world that involves powerful AI. It is not sufficient, right? There's no guarantee that a powerful AI system can protect you from a weapon created by an AI system. There's no guarantee that our institutions can adapt to a world where everyone is much more capable than they were before. But I think it is at least an important part of a hope and that is what this whole lecture will be about.
turns.zh: 我认为我们能描绘的任何美好世界都涉及人们能够获得强大的 AI，以减轻潜在的危害。至少任何涉及强大 AI 的美好世界都是如此。但这还不够，对吧？不能保证强大的 AI 系统能保护你免受 AI 系统制造的武器的伤害。不能保证我们的机构能适应一个人人都比过去更有能力的世界。但我认为这至少是希望的重要组成部分，而这就是整个讲座要讲的内容。

turns.en: So I'm going to talk a little while about why I think this problem is not solved by default. Why it requires some thought from us, why we need to treat it as a challenge to be addressed.
turns.zh: 所以我要花一点时间谈谈为什么我认为这个问题不会自动解决。为什么它需要我们思考，为什么我们需要把它当作一个需要应对的挑战。

turns.en: So one thing you might have hoped is just the market will fix this problem, right? The people want trustworthy AI. People want to be able to rely on the AI systems they use and so customers will push companies to build trustworthy AI. The problem with this is a solution. The reason why it is not a complete solution is that someone else's AI can hurt me. It's not enough to say that I won't adopt an AI if I can't trust it. I also stand to be influenced by someone else's AI carrying out a cyber attack or building a weapon or whatever else.
turns.zh: 所以你可能希望的一件事就是市场会解决这个问题，对吧？人们想要可信的 AI。人们希望能够依赖他们使用的 AI 系统，因此客户会推动公司构建可信的 AI。问题在于，这只是一个解决方案。它不是一个完整解决方案的原因是，别人的 AI 可能会伤害我。仅仅说如果我不信任 AI 就不会采用它是不够的。我也会受到别人的 AI 进行网络攻击或制造武器或其他行为的影响。

turns.en: So, a natural response in that world is to say, let us hold AI developers liable for some of the harms their systems cause. And I think this is an important step. I think clarifying liability can help improve practices in AI development. I think it can help cost benefits be weighed appropriately. But I don't think it can fix the whole problem. In particular, I think we can enter a regime where harms are much larger than our ability to pay. So over the last few nights, we have been talking about scales of harms that include killing large numbers of people or overthrowing governments, where the potential damages are orders of magnitude larger than the valuation of AI companies, where you have risks that you could not realistically ensure and which you can't expect developers to cover.
turns.zh: 所以，在那个世界里，一个自然的回应是，让 AI 开发者对其系统造成的某些危害负责。我认为这是一个重要的步骤。我认为明确责任可以帮助改善 AI 开发实践。我认为它可以帮助适当权衡成本效益。但我不认为它能解决整个问题。特别是，我认为我们可能会进入一个危害远大于我们支付能力的制度。所以在过去的几个晚上，我们一直在讨论危害的规模，包括杀死大量人或推翻政府，其中潜在损害比 AI 公司的估值大几个数量级，你面临的风险是你无法现实地确保的，也不能指望开发者承担。

turns.en: When we consider these extreme risks, you also run into this problem that if you're asking about AI systems potentially overthrowing states, it's not a helpful remedy after the fact to try and come in and sue them. So I think particularly if harms can concentrate in these tales, right? So we talked on Monday about how it is that AI systems might behave well while under human control while still running some risk of escaping human control in a catastrophic way. Those dynamics can push harms into this catastrophic tale which is particularly challenging to handle with a liability regime. And so I don't think markets even with liability address this problem automatically on their own. I think it's something that requires additional work even if markets and liability are important mechanisms.
turns.zh: 当我们考虑这些极端风险时，你还会遇到这个问题：如果你问的是 AI 系统可能推翻国家，事后试图起诉他们并不是有用的补救措施。所以我认为特别是如果危害可以集中在这些尾部，对吧？所以我们在周一谈到了 AI 系统如何在人类控制下表现良好，同时仍然存在以灾难性方式逃脱人类控制的风险。这些动态可以将危害推入这个灾难性的尾部，这对责任制度来说尤其具有挑战性。所以我认为市场即使有责任制度，也不会自动解决这个问题。我认为这是需要额外工作的事情，即使市场和责任是重要的机制。

turns.en: Another hope you can have is that incentivist be damned developers can just not build unsafe AI systems. Um I think at the level of a society this is maybe doesn't sound that plausible as a hope. uh there's the problem that there are many possible developers of AI products and they may not all be responsible and even if developers are responsible they may think to themselves if I don't do this someone else will right even if people are reasonably altruistic uh you can end up in a place where there are a lot of incentives to take risks and a lot of ability to explain how those risks aren't really hurting people aren't really contributing on the margin so I think at the level of society this is not a good solution to the problem
turns.zh: 另一个希望是，不管激励如何，开发者可以不构建不安全的 AI 系统。嗯，我认为在社会层面上，这听起来可能不太可信。有一个问题是，AI 产品可能有很多开发者，他们可能并不都负责任，即使开发者负责任，他们也可能想，如果我不这样做，别人也会这样做，对吧？即使人们相当利他，你最终可能会处于一个有很多冒险激励和很多能力来解释这些风险并没有真正伤害人们、并没有真正在边际上有所贡献的地方。所以我认为在社会层面上，这不是一个很好的解决方案。

turns.en: you could hope we can not think through the problem in advance we can deploy AI see what goes ong and then learn and iterate to address the particular problems that emerge. But we've already talked briefly about the challenges with this approach. Right? So AI may advance very quickly as we talked about last night. You may have a transition over a period of a few months or maybe one year from AI systems which can be integrated safely to those that pose catastrophic risks. And perhaps more importantly, this risk can be concentrated in the tail, right? Where maybe the first time something really catastrophic goes wrong, it is too late to remediate the problem after the fact.
turns.zh: 你可能希望我们不必提前思考问题，我们可以部署 AI，看看会发生什么，然后学习并迭代以解决出现的特定问题。但我们已经简要讨论了这种方法的挑战。对吧？所以 AI 可能发展得非常快，正如我们昨晚谈到的。你可能在几个月或也许一年的时间内从可以安全集成的 AI 系统过渡到构成灾难性风险的系统。也许更重要的是，这种风险可以集中在尾部，对吧？也许第一次真正灾难性的事情出错时，事后补救问题就太晚了。

turns.en: All of these difficulties would be less severe if we could apply the same approaches we apply in other technologies to AI. If we can say there is a test that everyone can agree upon that we already understand which you can run in order to determine if a system is safe for deployment. Uh but a problem is AI is sort of unlike any technology we have ever worked with before. Right? AI systems when tested can become aware that they are being tested. It is already the case that AI systems are very often aware that they are being tested. They modulate their behavior specifically based on beliefs about what an evaluator is looking for. Right? So we have this unprecedented sensitivity of the behavior of an AI system to features about its environment that make it extremely hard to say this test tells us about the performance in the cases we actually care about.
turns.zh: 如果我们能把我们在其他技术中应用的相同方法应用于 AI，所有这些困难都不会那么严重。如果我们能说有一个每个人都同意的测试，我们已经理解，你可以运行它来确定系统是否安全部署。但问题是 AI 有点不像我们以前合作过的任何技术。对吧？AI 系统在被测试时可能会意识到它们正在被测试。已经情况是，AI 系统经常意识到它们正在被测试。它们特别根据对评估者寻找什么的信念来调节它们的行为。对吧？所以我们有这种前所未有的 AI 系统行为对其环境特征的敏感性，这使得很难说这个测试告诉我们关于我们真正关心的情况下的表现。

turns.en: So all of that is to say I don't think this problem is easily addressed or is automatically addressed. I think this is a challenge that we actually need to step up to and take ownership on. So what do we need to know and what do we need to ensure if we want these systems to be safe? If we want defenders to be able to rely on Frontier AI models, I'm going to talk about five categories. The specification of their behavior, their alignment, their capabilities, our ability to control them, and security.
turns.zh: 所以所有这些都说明，我认为这个问题不容易解决，也不会自动解决。我认为这是一个我们真正需要站出来承担责任的挑战。那么，如果我们希望这些系统安全，我们需要知道什么，需要确保什么？如果我们希望防御者能够依赖前沿 AI 模型，我将谈论五个类别：它们行为的规范、它们的对齐、它们的能力、我们控制它们的能力，以及安全性。

turns.en: So first specification. So here the goal is people who rely on AI systems should have clear expectations about the behavior of a model. Right? Right? So this model that you right we're increasingly in a world where many people are relying on AI systems produced by potentially a small number of tech companies. Those systems are in some way very opaque. Uh people do not have direct visibility into how they are trained. We need to understand what should I expect that system to do if I want to rely on it. So this includes first what behavior is intended.
turns.zh: 首先是规范。所以这里的目标是，依赖 AI 系统的人应该对模型的行为有明确的期望。对吧？对吧？所以这个模型，你，对，我们越来越处于一个许多人依赖可能由少数科技公司生产的 AI 系统的世界。这些系统在某种程度上非常不透明。人们无法直接了解它们是如何训练的。我们需要理解，如果我想依赖它，我应该期望那个系统做什么。所以这首先包括预期的行为是什么。

turns.en: How does that system balance the conflicting interests of the user and the developer? How does it balance requests from the user with laws and norms? And then it also involves beyond just saying what behavior is intended, how is that actually operationalized in training? How does developer decide what behavior was actually the correct behavior to be reinforced?
turns.zh: 这个系统如何平衡用户和开发者之间相互冲突的利益？它如何平衡用户的请求与法律和规范？然后，这还涉及到不仅仅是说明意图行为是什么，而是如何在训练中实际实施？开发者如何决定什么行为实际上是被强化的正确行为？

turns.en: OpenAI publishes a document they call the model spec explaining how they think models should approach these choices. Anthropic calls it analogous document cloud's constitution. And these documents are intended to lay out here is how our systems are supposed to behave.
turns.zh: OpenAI 发布了一份他们称为模型规范的文件，解释他们认为模型应如何处理这些选择。Anthropic 称其类似文件为 Claude 的宪法。这些文件旨在阐明我们的系统应该如何行为。

turns.en: A second and perhaps even more important question is will models actually follow that specification. Right? If we want to rely upon them, this is critical. It doesn't matter if the intended behavior is good if in high-stakes settings those systems won't behave as intended. And so we face questions like first, how are these systems trained and evaluated? How did the system get how do developers try and cause the system to follow the specification? And how do they determine that they think it does? These are questions which only a developer often has the answer to. Right? I am not able to say as an outsider how a system was trained. I need access to additional information. With that information, I then face a very hard scientific question. Based on what I know about how the system was trained and evaluated, how likely is it to behave in a catastrophically misaligned way or a subtly misaligned way uh once deployed?
turns.zh: 第二个或许更重要的问题是，模型真的会遵循那个规范吗？对吧？如果我们想依赖它们，这一点至关重要。如果意图行为是好的，但在高风险环境中这些系统不按预期行为，那也没用。所以我们面临这样的问题：首先，这些系统是如何训练和评估的？开发者如何试图让系统遵循规范？他们又如何确定他们认为系统确实遵循了？这些问题的答案往往只有开发者知道。对吧？作为外部人，我无法说明系统是如何训练的。我需要获取额外信息。有了这些信息，我面临一个非常困难的科学问题：根据我对系统训练和评估方式的了解，它在部署后以灾难性错位或微妙错位方式行为的可能性有多大？

turns.en: And finally, you might like to know what kind of failures have we actually observed in practice when these systems are deployed. What incidents of misalignment, what patterns of behavior have we seen?
turns.zh: 最后，你可能想知道，当这些系统部署时，我们在实践中实际观察到了什么样的失败。我们看到了哪些错位事件，哪些行为模式？

turns.en: So these first two categories were understanding how a system is intended to behave, understanding whether a system actually behaves as intended, right? The scientific question.
turns.zh: 所以前两个类别是理解系统意图行为，理解系统是否实际按预期行为，对吧？科学问题。

turns.en: A third question is if a system does behave in an unintended way, can we detect and prevent harm? This includes questions like are we able to monitor and detect harm? So if a system is trying to cause trouble, is it the case that monitors can reliably detect those attempts before something bad actually happens? And then are monitors actually applied over relevant traffic and are they actually acted upon? Beyond monitoring, that's probably the single most important control right now in AI practice. There are other potential controls. And so we want to ask the slightly broader question. If a system was trying to cause harm given the way it is actually deployed, would it be able to do so without being detected and prevented?
turns.zh: 第三个问题是，如果系统确实以非预期方式行为，我们能否检测和预防伤害？这包括我们能否监控和检测伤害？所以，如果一个系统试图制造麻烦，监控器能否在坏事发生前可靠地检测到这些尝试？然后，监控器是否实际应用于相关流量，并且是否实际被采取行动？除了监控，这可能是目前 AI 实践中最重要的单一控制。还有其他潜在控制。所以我们想问一个稍微更广泛的问题：鉴于系统的实际部署方式，如果它试图造成伤害，它能否在不被发现和阻止的情况下做到？

turns.en: A fourth question is security. So I can tell a good story about how systems are intended to behave, how we trained them, and how safeguards protect us from harm. But that is not valuable unless those efforts actually function in the real world, including with the possibility of attack. And so we should do a similar red teaming exercise to ask, can an attacker undermine those safeguards? where an attacker might mean an external actor, an attacker might mean an insider or increasingly an attacker might mean a model involved in the development process as we discussed last night which has the intention of undermining safeguards.
turns.zh: 第四个问题是安全。所以我可以很好地讲述系统意图如何行为、我们如何训练它们以及保障措施如何保护我们免受伤害。但除非这些努力在现实世界中实际发挥作用，包括面对攻击的可能性，否则没有价值。因此，我们应该进行类似的红队演练，问：攻击者能否破坏这些保障措施？攻击者可能指外部行为者，也可能指内部人员，或者越来越多地指参与开发过程的模型，正如我们昨晚讨论的，该模型有意破坏保障措施。

turns.en: And the final category is capabilities. So I've talked about a number of safeguards, but the importance of those safeguards depends on how much can go wrong if a system fails. And as the capabilities of a system rise, the stakes increase significantly. the bar we need to hold ourselves to for alignment or control or security increases. And I want to call out two questions here. One is an understanding of what are the current dual use capabilities. So how effective is a system at cyber or how effective is a system at bio? Um but also what is the short-term trajectory of capabilities? So we talked last night about the possibility of recursive self-improvement leading to very rapid acceleration. That means that it can be important to know not just where are capabilities now but what have we seen about where capabilities might be even over a three or six month horizon because again these questions will shape how important is it that the systems are adequately aligned controlled and secured.
turns.zh: 最后一个类别是能力。所以我谈到了许多保障措施，但这些保障措施的重要性取决于系统失败时可能出多大问题。随着系统能力的提升，风险显著增加。我们对齐、控制或安全的标准也随之提高。我想在这里指出两个问题。一是了解当前的双重用途能力。那么系统在网络或生物方面的效能如何？但也要了解能力的短期轨迹。我们昨晚讨论了递归自我改进导致非常快速加速的可能性。这意味着，不仅要知道当前能力在哪里，还要了解我们在三个月或六个月的时间范围内看到的能力可能在哪里，这很重要，因为再次，这些问题将决定系统充分对齐、控制和安全的重要性。

turns.en: So when I talk about goals, safety goals, I really mean to span those five categories, right? We want to ask how can we achieve reasonable outcomes in alignment, control, security, specification at a bar that depends on capabilities. And for the rest of the talk, I'll be talking about how do we try and get there. I'll discuss a couple ingredients. uh one is transparency, the development of a shared bar for safety, approaches for verifying whether developers are meeting that bar and then mechanisms to prevent the development of uncontrollable AI to push developers to actually meet that bar. And I'll talk a little bit about both what we want and what is happening now.
turns.zh: 所以当我谈论目标、安全目标时，我实际上是指涵盖那五个类别，对吧？我们想问，如何在取决于能力的标准下，在对齐、控制、安全和规范方面实现合理的结果。在接下来的演讲中，我将讨论我们如何努力实现这一目标。我将讨论几个要素。一个是透明度，制定共同的安全标准，验证开发者是否达到该标准的方法，以及防止开发不可控 AI 的机制，以推动开发者真正达到该标准。我将简要谈谈我们想要什么以及现在正在发生什么。

turns.en: So first, transparency. The goal here is that the external world has enough information across all five of those areas I listed in order to understand the risks. So you would like to not be in the world where a developer is having internal analysis where a developer is able to say well I understand how the system was trained. If we want to have a shared bar, we ultimately need to have common understanding of what is being done. How do we tell whether controls are working? One step is companies publishing relevant information. Right? So they can disclose here are facts about how our system is trained. Here are facts about the capabilities of these systems, about the controls as they are implemented. This can be complemented by assessors who can provide summaries of sensitive details. So you might say there are facts about how a system is trained that developers are hesitant to publish. They might rely on working with third parties to collect that information and publish a summary while holding out proprietary information. uh and in general I think as a principle many of these questions depend on hard scientific discussions right if we want to understand does a given evaluation actually tell us that a system is aligned or was a given exercise actually enough to demonstrate that a control is effective those are hard scientific questions not settled science and in those cases I think discussions need to be public right we cannot have it be the case either that an AI developer is internally answering those questions with each developer arriving at separate answers in a very challenging systemic environment. Nor can it be the case that that occurs between some kind of third party behind closed doors with again very limited resources and limited public scrutiny. So I think a goal of transparency is both to understand what is happening and then for hard scientific questions to understand that the relevant evidence is available publicly for independent review.
turns.zh: 首先，透明度。这里的目标是外部世界在我列出的所有五个领域拥有足够的信息来理解风险。所以你不希望处于开发者进行内部分析、开发者能够说“嗯，我理解系统是如何训练的”这样的世界。如果我们想要有一个共同的标准，我们最终需要对正在做的事情有共同的理解。我们如何判断控制是否有效？一步是公司发布相关信息。对吧？所以他们可以披露：这是关于我们的系统如何训练的事实。这是关于这些系统能力的事实，关于已实施控制的事实。这可以由评估者提供敏感细节的摘要来补充。所以你可能会说，有些关于系统如何训练的事实开发者不愿发布。他们可能依赖与第三方合作收集信息并发布摘要，同时保留专有信息。总的来说，我认为作为一个原则，许多这些问题依赖于艰难的科学讨论，对吧？如果我们想理解给定的评估是否真的告诉我们系统是对齐的，或者给定的练习是否足以证明控制是有效的，这些都是艰难的科学问题，不是定论科学。在那些情况下，我认为讨论需要公开，对吧？我们不能出现这样的情况：一个 AI 开发者在内部回答这些问题，每个开发者在非常具有挑战性的系统环境中得出不同的答案。也不能出现这样的情况：这种情况发生在某种第三方闭门造车的情况下，同样资源有限，公众监督有限。所以我认为透明度的目标既是理解正在发生什么，然后对于艰难的科学问题，理解相关证据公开可用以供独立审查。

turns.en: The reason I'm so interested in transparency is I think it is the first step to actually arriving at something like a shared bar for safety. So I mentioned voluntary disclosures from companies. One form these take, perhaps the most important form right now, which people have probably seen, are either system cards associated with model releases or various forms of reporting on risk. So these are disclosures from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google. These are often quite large disclosures, right? They contain a lot of information about how systems are evaluated. They contain some information about how systems are trained and about control mechanisms that are in place. I think these are much better than a world with no disclosures. I think there would be a worse situation if people weren't able to discuss what was happening. But I would also emphasize that these disclosures currently do not have enough information for a member like an independent scientist to really form an independent view about risk. Right? The key questions are still being answered internally within AI companies or in other form.
turns.zh: 我对透明度如此感兴趣的原因在于，我认为这是真正达成某种共享安全标准的首要步骤。我提到了公司的自愿披露。这些披露目前最常见、或许也是最重要的形式，大家可能已经见过，就是与模型发布相关的系统卡，或者各种形式的风险报告。这些是来自 OpenAI、Anthropic、Google 的披露。这些披露通常相当庞大，对吧？它们包含大量关于系统如何被评估的信息，也包含一些关于系统如何训练以及现有控制机制的信息。我认为这比一个没有披露的世界要好得多。如果人们无法讨论正在发生的事情，情况会更糟。但我也要强调，这些披露目前还没有足够的信息，让像独立科学家这样的人真正形成对风险的独立看法。对吧？关键问题仍然在 AI 公司内部或以其他形式得到解答。

turns.en: I also mentioned this idea of third-party engagement. So here are a few engagements that have occurred on the topic of alignment. This is a subject close to my heart. I'm from METR and Apollo working with a number of frontier companies. And the goal of these engagements is to take in private information to try and produce a summary, explain the judgment, be methodologically transparent about that judgment, and to publish it without revealing some sensitive details that informed the judgment. Or in the case of these Apollo projects, to carry out research on models which are proprietary, to publish results from that research to help people understand without making the models themselves public, which I think we should think of as a supplement for these disclosures in cases where there are sensitive details.
turns.zh: 我还提到了第三方参与的想法。这里有一些在对齐主题上已经发生的参与。这是一个我关心的话题。我来自 METR 和 Apollo，与多家前沿公司合作。这些参与的目标是获取私有信息，尝试生成摘要，解释判断，在方法上对判断保持透明，并在不透露某些敏感细节的情况下发布，这些细节为判断提供了依据。或者在 Apollo 项目中，对专有模型进行研究，发布研究结果以帮助人们理解，而不公开模型本身，我认为在存在敏感细节的情况下，这应被视为这些披露的补充。

turns.en: The purpose of all of this transparency is to work towards a shared bar for safety again across all five of those categories that I mentioned or as a function of those five categories that I mentioned in the last section. So I think first that involves debate. I think people disagree a lot right now. There are incredible scientific disagreements about what evidence is actually enough to understand whether mitigation is working and what mitigations are actually necessary. How do you tell if a system is aligned based on an evaluation given that the system is likely to understand that it is being evaluated? That is a hard scientific question. Having those messy debates in public, having independent scientific review is a critical step towards getting to a reasonable view. I think even if you cannot reach perfect consensus, having some kind of shared bar is incredibly valuable for changing the incentive landscape. I think you're in a bad world if people are making independent decisions under an incredible financial incentive to be lax around themselves. Even if we cannot agree about exactly what level of evidence corresponds to what level of risk, simply having something we can agree upon, some reasonable standard that we can adopt, can help improve the situation. And I think right now, honestly, meeting any kind of scientifically defensible standard, getting into a world where we can say maybe some people disagree, but this is at least a reasonable picture. This is a reasonable statement, a reasonable way to evaluate that my system was working as intended, would be quite important.
turns.zh: 所有这些透明度的目的，是再次朝着我在上一节提到的所有五个类别或作为这五个类别的函数，努力达成共享的安全标准。所以我认为首先这涉及辩论。我认为现在人们有很多分歧。关于什么证据实际上足以理解缓解措施是否有效以及哪些缓解措施实际上是必要的，存在惊人的科学分歧。鉴于系统很可能理解自己正在被评估，你如何根据评估判断一个系统是否对齐？这是一个艰难的科学问题。在公开场合进行这些混乱的辩论，进行独立的科学审查，是朝着合理观点迈进的关键一步。我认为即使你无法达成完美共识，拥有某种共享标准对于改变激励格局也是非常有价值的。如果人们在巨大的财务激励下做出独立决定，对自己宽松，我认为你处于一个糟糕的世界。即使我们无法就什么水平的证据对应什么水平的风险达成一致，仅仅拥有一些我们可以同意的东西，一些我们可以采用的合理标准，也能帮助改善情况。而且我认为现在，老实说，达到任何科学上站得住脚的标准，进入一个我们可以说也许有些人不同意，但至少这是一个合理的图景的世界。这是一个合理的陈述，一种合理的方式来评估我的系统是否按预期工作，这将非常重要。

turns.en: So with some kind of safety bar in hand, the next step is verifying that a company's meeting it, right? We need some way to tell whether a developer is meeting that bar. Both we'll talk about enforcement mechanisms soon, but all of them will depend on some kind of visibility. So this can be a natural outgrowth of the kind of transparency measures I discussed in the last few sections. But it does also require additional work, right? Or you might need to carry out audits to confirm that an implementation is actually working as described, that the process is actually implemented as someone claimed. A lot of organizations work in this space doing some combination of evaluation and assessment and verification. Many of them are ultimately interested in serving a verification function.
